div.p: Locking protocols for hard-real-time systems have not generalized well from uniprocessors to multiprocessors. Bounding and reducing so-called "remote blocking" is widely recognized as an important problem for hard-real-time computing. W e describe a combination of locking and versioning protocols adapted from database concurrency control, together with a "chopping" analysis to shorten critical sections. Selective application of chopping and versioning reduces remote blocking and relaxes constraints imposed by pure locking protocols for multiprocessors. The protocol ensures 1 -version serializability. Using the same design-time information required for schedulability analysis in pure locking protocols, the mixed locking and versioning protocol can be implemented using only simple data structures with small bounded overheads and worst-case access times. W e illustrate the protocol with examples adapted f r o m the literature.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: During the past decade, considerable research has been done in bounding and reducing priority inversion or blocking for single-processor real-time systems. When resources are shared among tasks running on different processors, a task may have to wait for another task running on a different processor to release a locked resource. This waiting is referred to as remote blocking. It has been observed that the nature of blocking in a multiprocessor environment is quite different from that in a single-processor environment. Bounding and reducing remote blocking is widely recognized as an important problem for hard-real-time computing.

The priority ceiling protocol (PCP) has been extended to multiprocessors [RSL88] as a means of bounding remote blocking so that it is a function of the duration of executing critical sections of other remote tasks. A process migration technique is proposed [RSL88]: Whenever a task T enters a global critical section, this section of code is to be executed on a predesignated synchronization processor with a priority higher than those of the local tasks on the synchronization processor. Task T then relinquishes its execution right on the local processor and waits to be rescheduled on its local processor after its global critical section of code has been completed on the synchronization processor.

Since global critical sections are now executed on the same global processor, PCP can ensure that each global critical section will experience remote blocking as a function of the duration of executing global critical sections of higher and equal priority and at most one global critical section of lower priority. Total blocking time of a task includes suspension blocking caused by code migration, remote blocking caused by tasks on remote processors, and deferred blocking caused by deferred execution requests of higher priority tasks. (The latter problem has been addressed by Rajkumar, who eliminates deferred blocking by delaying the next release of a suspended task [RajSl].)

There are some problems associated with this migration scheme. First, although global critical sections can be pre-compiled on the synchronization processor (so migration is really a remote procedure call), copying some amount of processor states between the local and synchronization processor is generally unavoidable. Furthermore, on a local processor, blocking can be bounded to the duration of one critical section of a lower priority task. On a multiprocessor, a task may be "blocked" by higher priority tasks migrated from other processors as well, and it may experience blocking at each global critical section. The overall blocking duration that each task my experience therefore can be significant.
In this paper, we propose a mixed locking/versioning concurrency control protocol for multiprocessor RTS.

Our correctness criterion is serializability. The protocol has three parts: 0 A simple locking protocol is used for most data items. It may be implemented by priority elevation (e.g., read-write priority ceiling proto-
or by delayed execution (stack-based scheduling [Bakgl]) when conflicts are between processes that share a processor.

Versioning can be selectively applied to remove read-write conflicts. Inexpensive implementations of versioning are made possible by designtime knowledge of task rates and data requirements, and the effectiveness of versioning in reducing conflicts is enhanced by "chopping" update transactions into query and update phases.

0 When remote blocking is removed by our versioning scheme, the simple priority inversion control technique, i.e., interrupt disabling, is used when executing versioning-related short critical sections.

The information required for resolving conflicts is the same information needed for schedulability analysis with pure locking protocols such as readlwrite priority ceiling protocol. Most importantly, the mixed lockinglversioning protocol can be used to reduce worstcase blocking rather than some probabilistic measure, and it can be used to alleviate the critical problem of remote blocking in multi-processor real-time systems.

One important property of our protocol is that if all remote conflicts can be resolved by versioning and chopping, then we will not need to migrate global critical sections to synchronization processors. This is very important in terms of reducing remote blocking because tasks in this case will not be blocked by other global critical sections on the synchronization processors. By executing versioning-related critical sections without interruption, tasks do not suspend and hence the consequent problems of suspension blocking and deferred blocking can be avoided entirely. The protocol does have a constraint though: all versioned data written by a task must reside on the same processor. This is necessary to guarantee atomic commitment for updaters, which in turn is needed to guarantee serializability. This constraint can be mitigated by using appropriate data allocation schemes.

div.head: Model and assumptions
div.p: The research described in this paper assumes the computation model of a general shared-memory multiprocessor system running real-time applications. We will consider each task to be a sequence of zero or more transactions, where a transaction is a sequence of operations including reads and writes of non-local data, and is a unit of consistency and scheduling. Each task is either periodic occuring at regular intervals or aperiodic with a known minimum interval arrival time.

Tasks are assumed to be statically allocated to processors. Intertask communication is realized through implementation of shared data objects. However, tasks sharing the same data are not necessarily running on the same processor. On each processor, tasks are to be scheduled on a priority basis. Static priority preemptive scheduling is assumed and fixed priorities are assigned to tasksed. Hence, a task will be running with its assigned priority unless being temporarily assigned a new priority for reasons for concurrency control.

The correctness criterion we will establish is sem'alizability, which essentially means maintaining an illusion that each transaction executes atomically. The attraction of serializability is simple: It permits local reasoning about transactions as atomic units. Whether one reasons formally or informally about program correctness, considering each transaction individually rather than explicitly considering their possible interleavings is nearly essential to avoiding subtle errors.

div.head: Approach
div.p: It is difficult t o reduce worst-case remote blocking in a pure locking protocol. An alternative is to use versioning to eliminate some conflicts entirely. We describe an integrated protocol in which versioning can be applied selectively to remove conflicts that lead to excessive blocking. Because versioning can be applied selectively, with locking protocols for other data, it is particularly well suited as a trouble-shooting method to minimize remote blocking in order to satisfy tasks' schedulability requirements.

div.head: The basic version pool algorithm
div.p: Our starting point is the version pool algorithm [CFL+82], an extension of the two-phase locking protocol (2PL) which combines locking and versioning. It can be considered as a formalization of the common practice of buffering data to reduce contention, but in contrast to ad hoc buffering practices it ensures the rather strong consistency property of 1-version serializable execution (lSR), i.e., the interleaved execution of transactions on data that may have multiple copies is equivalent to a serial execution of those transactions on single-copy data.

The version pool algorithm distinguishes read-only transactions from transactions that update the data base. (We discuss in Section 4.2 how parts of updating tasks can be transformed into read-only transactions.) Update transactions are scheduled by 2PL; updates do not overwrite the original values but create new versions. When an update transaction T commits, it obtains a timestamp and attaches the timestamp to all versions created by r. A query q obtains a timestamp at the start of its execution. Whenever q accesses a data item x, it searches for the most recent version of 2 with a timestamp smaller than q's timestamp. Since queries do not acquire locks, they do not interfere with other queries or with updaters. Unlike "optimistic" timestamp-ordering protocols, there is no runtime validation phase nor are transactions ever aborted.

This protocol removes a class of blocking, hence is advantageous when blocking is a significant factor in schedulability. The simple implementation described in Section 3.2.1 has small space and time overheads that can be bounded at design time, given the same information about task rates required for schedulability analysis. Selective application of versioning as discussed below makes these overheads even more acceptable.

div.head: Implementation issues
div.p: Schedulability analysis requires that every overhead in a scheduling protocol be bounded. In addition, operations in the protocol that must be executed atomically must be minimized, since priority inversion and remote blocking will occur for the duration of these operations.

The overheads of the integrated protocol are due mainly to versioning. (Acquiring timestamps is also an overhead, but low-cost means for accomplishing this are well known.) Versioning may be implemented in a variety of ways, with different performance characteristics. Since schedulability analysis depends on worstcase behavior, we must show that the protocol admits an implementation with small, bounded overheads. In particular, we must consider allocation and reclama-

div.head: Bounding space and execution costs tion of version storage and bounding the time a query must search for a proper version.
div.p: Some hard real-time systems are composed of periodic tasks which cycle forever; critical aperiodic tasks are associated with periods using cyclic "server" tasks [SSL89]. We can take advantage of the repetitive nature of periodic tasks by allocating versions of each object in a simple ring buffer.

We must bound the size required for each buffer to prevent query access to "reclaimed" (overwritten) buffer cells. No explicit reclamation is required if the relative rates of queries and updaters are known.

As a result, with respect to task q, + 2 cells must be allocated in the ring buffer for x. Writes likewise are constant-time operations. Reads scheduled by timestamps require searching the ring buffer. Since 2PL of updaters ensures that versions will be maintained in chronological order, each versioned read will be a simple linear search of versions written between query initiation and the time of the versioned read. If the relative rates of queries and updaters are too large, an ISAM-like secondary index may be built (also allocated from a ring buffer), giving a worst-case search time of 2 f l steps, where V is the linear search time; this should be an acceptable delay even for remote reads, which can simply spin while the read is executed on a synchronization processor.

div.head: Atomic initiation and commitment
div.p: The version pool algorithm ensures serializability only if the commitment stage of an updater is atomic. It would be unacceptable in HRTS for low-priority updaters to block higher-priority tasks by an amount of time proportional to the number of items the updater writes (as would result from a simple delayed-write scheme.) To bound the time for atomic commitment independent of the number of items modified, provided all versioned data written by a task resides on the same processor (we discuss a method to mitigate this constraint in Section 4.3), we associate with each updater a timestamp node (also allocated from a ring buffer). Each cell in the version buffer stores the value of a created data version and a pointer to the timestamp node of the updater which created the data version. The indirection allows all items created by an updater to point to the same timestamp node, which can record the value "uncommitted" until the updater atomically obtains and writes the timestamp in constant time. The timestamp can be acquired on a remote processor holding the versioned data (again while spinning on the local processor). An updater cannot write versioned data on more than one processor without incurring unacceptable additional blocking, but this is unlikely t o be a problem if versioning is applied selectively as we have described.

div.head: Extension of the basic protocol
div.p: We extend the version pool algorithm in three ways. First, we make the simple observation that versioning can be applied selectively to minimize overhead. Second, we note that transactions can be transformed into smaller critical sections using a "chopping graph" analysis due to Shasha. Chopped queries can be scheduled without blocking using timestamps like ordinary queries. Third, write-write conflicts can be removed by using a separate version buffer for each updater that writes versioned data.

div.head: Selective versioning
div.p: The version pool algorithm was designed as if it were applied to every datum in an entire system. Especially attractive, though, is an observation that a pure locking protocol is a degenerate case of the integrated protocol. Any query transaction can be treated as an updater and scheduled using 2PL. If every task that accesses a datum uses 2PL, then that datum requires neither versions nor timestamps. Likewise, only queries that read versioned data and updaters that write versioned data need obtain timestamps; an updater that reads versioned data (and optionally singleversion data as well) and writes only single-version data executes exactly as in a pure locking protocol. When reasoning about serializability, we consider every transaction to have a timestamp, but for the majority of transactions these timestamps are merely auxiliary variables with no physical existence and no cost.

If a system is "almost" schedulable under a pure locking protocol such as the read/write priority ceiling protocol, with only a few tasks rendered unschedulable by potential blocking, then it is sufficient to add versioning to only the data responsible for that blocking. Only tasks that access this critical data need obtain or use timestamps. There is a small amount of 'Lpropagation" of versioning, since a query that reads with timestamps must read only versioned data, but this propagation extends no further (versioning data does not force transactions to use versions). Other tasks incur no additional time or space overhead.

div.head: Chopping transactions
div.p: Versioning removes read/write conflict between a query and an updater, but not between a writer of item
x and a task that reads x t o update another item y.
Fortunately, under some circumstances it is possible to "chop" an updating task into a query subtransaction followed by an updating subtransaction.

The chopping graph proposed by Shasha et al. in [SSV92] provides a method for chopping transactions into smaller scheduling units. Each piece of a chopped transaction is represented by a node in the chopping graph. An S (sibling) edge connects each pair of pieces of the same transaction. A C (conflict) edge connects any two nodes of different transactions if the two nodes contain conflicting operations, i.e., if they operate on the same datum and at least one of them is write. After the chopping graph is constructed, we combine pieces of transactions until there is no cycle containing both S and C edges.

Shasha et al. have shown that with such a transformation, executions are guaranteed to be serializable if each transaction or subtransaction is scheduled by 2PL. We have shown ISY951 that the same chopping guarantee holds for chopping in combination with any multiversion serializable scheduler, including the version pool algorithm. In particular, when we chop between the reading and writing part of an updating transaction, the reading part becomes a query transaction which can read versioned data without obtaining a lock. Since locking is a degenerate case of the version pool algorithm, and since (as we discuss below) locking, chopping, and versioning can co-exist, we can apply chopping and versioning as a trouble-shooting technique to resolve excessive blocking in order to satisfy tasks' schedulability requirements.

Chopping may be adequate to reduce worst-case blocking even without versioning. If a transaction is chopped into smaller pieces, it implies that the duration that locks are held will be shortened; in particular, changing nested critical sections to a sequence of individual critical sections can dramatically reduce worstcase blocking.' Since chopping can be applied without extra runtime cost, it is the preferred trouble-shooting technique when schedulability analysis reveals excessive blocking overheads.

In a multiprocessor environment, there is a great difference between reducing the duration of remote blocking and removing it entirely. When a combination of chopping and versioning is used to eliminate remote blocking on a data item, it also eliminates suspension blocking, deferred blocking, and the necessity of process migration.

div.head: Removing Write-Write Conflicts
div.p: Others have noted [Gra93, Jef92, ABRW921 that embedded real-time systems often have a data-flow like character in which each data item is written by only a single task. To the extent that this is true, write-write conflicts will be rare. Nonetheless, we also consider a simple technique to remove write-write conflicts.

The version-pool algorithm requires that a write lock be set before creating a new version. The write locks will block concurrent reads, which is crucial in the protocol's correctness proof. The write locks will also block concurrent writes, which is essential to bounding the search times for queries in the ring buffers as explained in Section 3.2.1. Read locks exclude concurrent writes so that each read can always access the most recent version of an item.

We can remove write-write conflicts by using a separate ring buffer for each updater and for each versioned datum (previously one buffer for one versioned datum shared by all updaters). Using a separate version buffer for each updater that writes versioned data not only reduces the write-write conflicts, but also mitigates the constraint imposed by our implementation of the protocol as we described in Section 3.2.2, i.e., all versioned data written by a task must reside on the same processor.

'This is the same motivation as for the atomic data set method proposed by Sha [SRL88, SLJ881, which also has the effect of allowing a long transaction to be broken into shorter critical sections. Unlike atomic data sets, chopping does not restrict or weaken the consistency criterion.

Each updater will maintain versions of a datum in timestamp order in its own ring buffer. The commitment stage of an updater should still be atomic. A query will then search for the proper version of a datum x from all of the ring buffers of x. Each read in an updater can locate the most recent version also by checking each ring buffer.

Note that each transaction will read versions from other transactions with smaller timestamps because write locks still block concurrent reads and because the same rules are used for version selection for queries. Furthermore, reads in updaters will access the most recent version of each datum because read and write on the same datum are still mutually exclusive. Each query will still read the youngest versions that are older than the query itself because (1) the commitment stage of an updater is atomic (2) the same rules are used for version selection for queries.

There will be extra overheads in using multiple buffers because a query will need to access more than one buffer pointer value instead of just one as in the shared-buffer case. Accessing versions through secondary indexes will also take longer time.

div.head: Compatibility
div.p: It is important to verify the correctness of this extension. For ease of reference, we show the compatibility relationships of the various access methods of our protocol in Table 1 and explain our protocol rules below.

div.head: Integrated protocol rules
div.p: Based on our discussion above, integrating versioning and locking in the same protocol is made possible because we can choose each datum to be either oneversion( 1V) or multi-version(MV), and then determine an appropriate access method, based on Table 1, for each operation in a transaction. Following, when an updater or query is mentioned, we mean either the original transaction or a chopped sub-transaction.

Queries (read-only transactions) can be scheduled either by timestamps or 2PL, but the entire query must be scheduled by the same mechanism. If timestamp is to be used, then all data items accessed by the query must be versioned (MV). If any item is single version (lV), then the query will be scheduled by 2PL. A query can be scheduled by 2PL even if all accessed items are MV.

If a query uses timestamps, it obtains its timestamp at initiation; each read(x) will read the most recent version of x with a timestamp smaller than the query's timestamp. If a query uses 2PL, it obtains read-locks For each write operation in an updater, a write-lock on x is first obtained. If x is MV, then write(x) creates a new version of x. Otherwise, the value of x is overwritten.

At commitment, the updater obtains a timestamp and assigns that timestamp to all created versions atomically. If all the data written were lV, then the timestamp is again an auxiliary variable that need not actually be obtained.

We have assumed that each transaction acquires a timestamp either at their initiation (if scheduled by timestamp) or at their commit time (if scheduled by 2PL). This assumption is used to reason about a total order of timestamps among conflicting transactions, which in turn guarantees that all schedules are 1SR.

div.head: Applying the protocol
div.p: We illustrate our protocol with two examples adapted from the literature below.

Example 1. (from [RSL88]) Assuming there are four tasks 7-1, 7 2 , 7-3, and 7-4. The priorities of tasks are such that task 71 has highest priority, then tasks 7 -2 , ~. Task 7-4 has lowest priority. Suppose that tasks 7 1 , 7 2 and 7-3 are bound to processor p 2 and that task 74 is bound to processor pl (see Figure 1.) Task 7-4 is executing on processor p l and attempts to lock semaphore S. But S is currently locked by task 73 executing on processor pa. However, if 7-1 now preempts 7-3 on processor pa, 7-4 will be blocked until arriving higher priority tasks on pa (such as 7-1 and 7-2) complete execution or suspend themselves. Since 7 1 and 7 2 are periodic tasks, the blocking duration of 74 can be extremely long.

Priority inheritance or ceiling protocols can not improve this situation since task 7-4 has the lowest priority of the four tasks in the example. Because semaphore S guards a global critical section, the solution given in [RSL88] is to schedule the global critical section of 74 on p 2 (as a synchronization processor) at a priority higher than local tasks 7 1 and 72.

We can further reduce blocking caused by task migration with the versioning protocol. Suppose semaphore S guards the use of a datum x, and task 7-4 needs to update its value while task 7-3 must retrieve its value. We first version x. 7 3 is a query with respect to x and its atomic action now is to obtain a timestamp when it starts (the actual read may interleave freely with respect to writing or updating transactions.) 7 3 executes the atomic action with highest priority on pro-cessor p2 and does not suspend itself if blocked. 74, a writer of x, will need to attach a timestamp to x when it commits (also in an atomic action). If 74 is blocked by 73% atomic action, the blocking time will be very short. Also, because 7 3 does not migrate, it will not take additional suspension and deferred blocking as in [RSL88].
Example 2. We annotate a portion of Audsley's example from [ABRW92] with its chopping graph in Fig-
ure 2. The S (sibling) edges in the chopping graph represent places where we must continue to hold a readlock if the edge is part of a cycle also containing C
edges, but where otherwise the task can be broken into a query sub-transaction followed by an updater.

An SC-cycle is formed if (unlike Audsley) we posit an external observer requiring a serializable view of the FuelLAvail and Ballast-Pump items. Otherwise, the S edges can be "chopped." Suppose tasks PortLevelProc and BallastDiff are allocated on one processor while tasks Star-boardLevelProc and FuelLevel are on another processor. We have the following situations: e There is a remote read-write conflict between tasks PortLevelProc and FuelLevel on item Port Level.
e There is a remote read-write conflict between tasks StarboardLevelProc and BallastDiff on item StarboardLevel.
e Both tasks FuelLevel and BallastDiff are updaters.

To remove remote read-write conflicts, we must first chop each of FuelLevel and BallastDiff into a query subtransaction followed by a writing subtransaction. We are able to do this since the corresponding chopping graph does not contain SC cycles (see Figure 2.) We can then version both Port Level and StarboardLevel to eliminate read-write conflicts. By doing so, we no longer need to migrate global critical sections embedded in the four tasks, meaning reduced remote blocking. In addition, we also alleviate the problem of forbidding global critical sections containing local critical sections in tasks FuelLevel and BallastDiff when FuelAvail is a local data item on the same processor that task FuelLevel resides and BallastPump is a local item on the same processor that task BallastDiff resides.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: Hard real-time systems must maintain data consistency as well as satisfy timing constraints. We have adapted and extended a concurrency control protocol based on locking and versioning with the enhancement of chopping transactions into smaller critical sections. The protocol is intended as a trouble-shooting tool when schedulability of the system cannot be guaranteed by a pure locking protocol like readlwrite priority ceiling protocol. The suitability of the protocol for trouble-shooting is based on the co-existence of locking and versioning in a single protocol, with selective application of versioning only where required to meet schedulability goals.

The integrated protocol ensures serializable executions, meaning that the illusion of atomic execution of transactions is maintained despite interleaved and parallel executions. Chopping should be used first to reduce critical section sizes. Versioning can be used selectively to further reduce readlwrite conflicts. Writewrite conflicts can be reduced with separate version buffers for updaters.

Removing conflicts for remote data access greatly shortens worst-case blocking during access and eliminates deferred and suspension blocking as well. Moreover, some restrictions of a pure locking-based version of the multiprocessor priority ceiling protocol can be relaxed. Overheads for versioning are small (and chopping is free), and every delay and overhead in the integrated locking/versioning protocol can be bounded at design time using the same information about task rates that is already required for schedulability analysis.
For future work, we plan to extend the protocol to deal with sporadic tasks. Also, we will study the performance of the protocol for different transaction mixes.

div.head: Finding The Critical Path in a Time-Constrained Workflow * 1 Introduction
div.p: In a highly competitive business landscape, organizations want to enhance customer service, product quality and overall efficiency. This forcibly makes them rely on enterprise-wide integration of information using advanced technologies like database systems, client-server computing, object-oriented methodologies and the World Wide Web. Amidst this trend, the concept of a workflow has emerged in an objective of automating and computerizing business processes in whole or part, which gives us many benefits as follows: structural efficiency of business process, performance improvement of business process, flexibility, better process control, improved customer service, etc.

A workflow is defined as "an automated procedure where documents, information or tasks are passed between partic-*This work was supported by grant No. 1999-1-303-007-3 from the interdisciplinary Research program of the KOSEF ipants according to a defined set of rules to achieve, or contribute to, an overall business goal" [6]. It is "a collection of activities" that are interconnected by sequence, alternative, or other workflow control structures. A Workflow Management System (WFMS) completely defines, manages and executes "workflows" through the execution of software whose order of execution is driven by a computer representation of the workflow logic [6].

Since many business processes which are abstracted to workflows have time constraints such as deadlines, time management is an important issue in connection with workflow performance [7][8]. In this paper we call these kinds of workflows time-constrained workflows. In general, deadlines of a workflow and its component activities are specified during workflow build-time. If a workflow instance violates the activity deadline during workflow execution, workflow management systems may make it escalated

[4] [3]. Because escalation generally includes compensations of already completed activities, it wastes shared system resources and incurs additional costs to workflow management systems, resulting in low workflow performance.

Figure 1 depicts a simple long-distance telephone call process with deadlines. A local exchange is an interface to the caller and the receiver of a telephone call, and a toll exchange is a mediator connecting two local exchanges or passing the telephone call to another toll exchange. In a district, there are a toll exchange and several local exchanges managed by the toll exchange. Each local exchange covers some areas in the district. The telephone call process has its overall completion time as the workflow deadline, i.e., from making a phone call to starting a conversation. And, each step has the activity deadline such as the maximum dialing time in Step 1, computing time in Step 2 and 3, and waiting time for the receiver in Step 7. Because telephone lines between a local exchange and a toll exchange or among toll exchanges are limited, Step 4, 5, and 6 have the maximum waiting time for the connection as their activity deadlines.
